opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that you can't run the full suite of evaluations continuously. They're expensive and take time, and some of them involve people actually sitting down and trying to get the model to do dangerous things. So you have to decide how often to check in, and the core worry is a capability jump between two evaluations where you'd cross a threshold without noticing.

The way we've approached it is to tie the intervals to how much the model could plausibly have changed, rather than just to the calendar. Effective compute is a reasonable proxy. If you've scaled up a meaningful amount since your last check, say something like a fourfold increase, that's a natural point to re-run things. But compute isn't the only way models get better. Improvements in fine-tuning, scaffolding, and elicitation techniques can unlock capabilities in a model that was already there. So there's also a time-based component: even if you haven't trained a bigger model, after a few months of algorithmic and post-training progress you should look again.

The other important piece is building in a buffer. You don't want your evaluation threshold to sit exactly at the point where the model becomes dangerous. You want the warning sign to trigger well before that, so that even if capabilities grow faster than you expected between checkpoints, you've left yourself room. So we try to design the evals to fire at a lower capability level than the one we're actually worried about, with a margin sized to the gap between evaluations.

Then there's the question of how hard you try to elicit capabilities. A model can seem safe just because you didn't prompt it well. If someone else comes along with better techniques later, the capability was latent the whole time. So part of the buffer is accounting for the fact that our own elicitation is imperfect.

Honestly, a lot of this is still being figured out. The intervals are a judgment call informed by scaling laws and by how quickly we've seen capabilities emerge in practice. As we learn more about how predictable these jumps are, I expect the specifics to change. But the principle stays the same: check often enough, and conservatively enough, that you never find out after the fact that you crossed a line.

r002.rationale: It ties evaluation intervals to effective-compute changes and gives a fourfold increase as an example, but does not connect that jump to a subjectively noticeable increase in model intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not state that Anthropic is uncertain about the effective-compute gap between yellow-line and red-line capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says warning evaluations should trigger well before the dangerous capability threshold, with a margin for faster-than-expected capability growth between checkpoints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I think people find a little counterintuitive about the RSP. The core idea is that you have these capability thresholds, and you want to make sure that a model doesn't cross one of them without you noticing and having the right safeguards in place. And the question is: how often do you have to check?

The way we approach it is basically a trigger based on effective compute. So rather than saying "we'll evaluate every six months" or something calendar-based, we say that any time the amount of effective compute used to train a model increases by a certain factor relative to the last model we evaluated — we've used a 4x jump as the number — that triggers a new round of evaluations. And then there's also a time-based backstop, so that if it's been a while since the last evaluation, we run them anyway, even if we haven't crossed that compute threshold. The reason for the backstop is that capabilities can improve through things that aren't captured in raw compute — algorithmic improvements, better data, post-training, elicitation techniques getting better — so you don't want to rely purely on compute as your signal.

Why 4x? The intuition is that you want the gap between evaluations to be small enough that the model couldn't plausibly jump from "clearly below the threshold" to "well past the threshold" within one interval. Capabilities tend to improve fairly smoothly as a function of compute, so if your last evaluation showed you comfortably below the line, a 4x increase is unlikely to get you dramatically over it. And critically, the evaluations themselves are designed with that buffer in mind — we're not testing "is this model at the dangerous capability level," we're testing "is this model within one interval's worth of progress of that level." So you set the evaluation bar conservatively, below the actual threshold you care about, precisely because you know you'll go some period without checking again.

The other thing I'd say is that this is hard to get exactly right, and I think of it as a judgment call that you want to revisit. If you pick the interval too long, you risk training a model past a threshold without realizing it. If you pick it too short, you're constantly running evaluations, which is expensive and slows things down, and you might end up in a world where the evals become a box-ticking exercise rather than something you take seriously. So there's a real tradeoff. And part of what the RSP is supposed to do is make that reasoning explicit and public, so that if we got it wrong — if it turned out capabilities were jumping faster than we expected per unit of compute — that would be visible and we'd have a reason to tighten it.

And honestly, the part I think is most important is the piece people sometimes skip over, which is that the policy is a commitment that if you do hit a threshold, you stop and don't deploy or keep scaling until the safety measures are actually in place. The interval question is really in service of that — it's just about making sure you catch the crossing in time to honor the commitment.

r001.rationale: The response mentions algorithmic improvements as a source of capability gains outside raw compute, but does not say effective compute credits such improvements or that they lower loss without additional training compute.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation rounds are triggered by a 4x increase in effective compute, but does not connect that jump to a subjectively noticeable increase in model intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss uncertainty about the effective-compute gap between yellow-line and red-line capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says evaluations use a conservative buffer below the actual threshold, but does not say yellow-line thresholds must sit substantially below red-line capabilities because models may significantly overshoot between evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how much could the model improve before we evaluate it again? You want the evaluations close enough together that you wouldn’t cross a consequential capability threshold and only discover that much later.

So I wouldn’t think of it primarily as a fixed number of weeks. It depends on how quickly capabilities are changing, what you expect from the next stage of training, and how much uncertainty there is in your evaluations. If you’re comfortably below a threshold, you can afford a larger interval. As you get closer, or if progress is surprising, you need to evaluate more frequently.

There’s a tradeoff, because evaluations take time and resources. But the interval needs to leave enough margin to detect that you’re approaching a threshold and put the required safeguards in place before you cross it.

r002.rationale: It recommends more frequent evaluations as capabilities approach thresholds, but does not state that Anthropic sets intervals using effective-compute jumps tied to noticeable increases in intelligence.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention yellow-line or red-line capabilities or uncertainty about the effective-compute gap between them.

r004.rationale: It says evaluations should leave margin before crossing a threshold, but does not explain that yellow-line warnings need to sit substantially below red-line capabilities because models may overshoot between evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: how much could the model improve before we evaluate it again? A fixed amount of calendar time isn’t necessarily a good measure, because progress can be quite uneven. You want the interval to be short enough that you’re unlikely to cross a capability threshold and go substantially beyond it without noticing.

So you need some margin. If an evaluation suggests you’re below a threshold, you shouldn’t interpret that as permission to make an arbitrarily large jump in capabilities before checking again. You have to account for uncertainty in the evaluation and uncertainty about how much improvement the next stage of training will produce.

There’s a practical tradeoff, because evaluations take time and resources. But as you get closer to a threshold, or become less confident about where the model sits, the case for evaluating more frequently gets stronger. The goal is to have the relevant safeguards in place before the capabilities that require them arrive.
